variants.a: Use case: stylized-concept. Original NPC pixel-art style exploration for a classic-inspired fantasy RPG, not an existing character or a copied game sprite. Produce ONE goblin, full body, strictly FRONT FACING, centered and standing idle with both feet planted, arms held a little away from the torso so the silhouette can later be animated in multiple directions. Common design: moss-green skin, large pointed ears, angular long nose, slightly hunched shoulders, wiry arms, broad hands and bare feet, simple ragged brown waistcloth with a rope belt, bare chest, no weapon or other props. Game sprite, not a portrait or chibi mascot. Slight view down onto the top of the feet, otherwise square front view. Important native target: 128x128 pixels; character approximately 90-104 pixels tall with generous transparent margin. Deliver as an 8x NEAREST-NEIGHBOR enlarged view of that native sprite on a 1024x1024 transparent canvas: intentional pixel clusters aligned to an 8-pixel grid, crisp stepped edges, no anti-aliasing, no tiny subpixel detail, no blur, no gradients. Clearly pixel art but neither extremely blocky nor a highly polished modern illustration. Rough handmade charm and readable body structure. No text, labels, scenery, frame, ground shadow or background. Style A: earthy and primitive. Broad irregular pixel clusters, no continuous dark contour outline; silhouettes defined mostly by dark green shadow planes. Limited palette of around 16-20 opaque colors. Two or three rough hand-placed shades per material, slightly lumpy anatomy and understated facial details. Deliberately homespun early computer RPG character artwork, retaining readable hands, face, and knees. Avoid slick highlights and decorative details.

No glossy specular shading, no smooth painting, no cute big eyes.
